nameStory: Brazilian elodea gets its name from its South American origins, hailing from Brazil, Argentina, Chile, and Uruguay. The name 'elodea' comes from the Greek word 'helodes,' meaning 'marshy' or 'swampy,' perfectly describing this aquatic plant's love of watery homes. It's also called large-flowered waterweed because its blooms are notably bigger than its North American cousins.
description: Brazilian elodea is a submerged aquatic plant that grows entirely underwater except for its small white flowers that pop up to the surface. This invasive species forms dense underwater forests with its branching stems that can grow several feet long. The whole plant has a bright green, almost artificial-looking appearance that makes it popular in aquarium stores. Unfortunately, when released into New England waters, it can quickly take over and crowd out native aquatic plants.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Bright green leaves arranged in whorls of 4-8 around the stem, each leaf about an inch long with a crisp, almost plastic-like texture when you handle them underwater

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white flowers with three petals that float on the water surface, noticeably larger than other waterweed flowers, blooming in summer

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense underwater colonies with long, branching stems that can completely fill shallow areas, creating thick underwater tangles

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, green stems that feel firm and crisp when broken, with a clean snap rather than a stringy tear

idTips.label: Roots
idTips.description: Often grows as floating fragments without roots, though it can develop white, thread-like roots when settled in sediment

habitat: Found in ponds, lakes, slow-moving streams, and quiet backwaters throughout New England, typically in water 3-10 feet deep. Prefers nutrient-rich waters and can tolerate a wide range of water conditions, which helps it spread rapidly. Often discovered in areas near residential developments where aquarium contents may have been dumped.

seasonality.spring: New growth begins as water warms, with fresh bright green shoots emerging from overwintering fragments or established colonies.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with rapid expansion and small white flowers appearing at the surface. This is when colonies are most visible and identifiable.
seasonality.fall: Growth slows but plants remain green and identifiable underwater, beginning to fragment as cooler weather arrives.
seasonality.winter: Dies back significantly in northern areas but may persist under ice as dormant fragments, ready to regrow when spring returns.

funFact: This aquatic invader is so aggressive that a single small fragment dropped from a fishing boat or dumped from an aquarium can establish an entirely new colony that covers acres within just a few years!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with our native Canadian waterweed, but Brazilian elodea has more leaves per whorl (4-8 vs 3-4) and much denser growth that forms thick underwater mats. Remember: if the underwater plant looks almost too green and perfect, like artificial aquarium plants, it's probably the Brazilian invader.
contextualKnowledge: This plant highlights a major conservation problem - the aquarium trade introducing invasive species to native waters. Many people don't realize that dumping aquarium contents into local ponds and streams can cause serious ecological damage that lasts for decades.
compareHints: Brazilian elodea grows much more densely than Canadian waterweed and has more leaves per whorl around the stem. While Canadian waterweed forms loose, scattered colonies, Brazilian elodea creates thick underwater forests that can completely choke out native species. The Brazilian species also has notably larger flowers and a brighter, more artificial-looking green color.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Canadian Waterweed has leaves consistently arranged in whorls of three, while its cousin Nuttall's Waterweed typically has 2-4 leaves per whorl and denser branching.
Nuttall's waterweed differs from Canadian waterweed mainly by having leaves in groups of three instead of four, and it tends to be slightly smaller overall.
